title: Work 25 minutes. Break. Repeat.
description:
Work 25 minutes. Break. Repeat. The man who invented it calls that a distortion. 'The iconic 25-minute sessions,' Francesco Cirillo writes, 'aren't the technique. They're just one expression of it.'

A university student who could not concentrate, timing himself with the first thing to hand on the kitchen counter: a wind-up timer shaped like a tomato. Pomodoro is simply Italian for tomato.

Not 25 minutes. Two. 'Can I study for just two minutes without interruption?' The famous 25 came later, and even that, he says, is one expression of the method, not the point of it.

His answer: even none is fine. 'Your goal isn't to complete Pomodoros,' he says, 'it's to become aware of what happens in your mind.' A focus method whose own author does not care how much you get done.

Sources:
- https://www.pomodorotechnique.com/francesco-cirillo/ (Francesco Cirillo's official site; read in full 26 Aug 2026): in his own words, 'I created the Pomodoro Technique in the 1980s with a tomato-shaped kitchen timer and a problem: I couldn't focus on my university studies', and the first experiment was 'Can I study for just two minutes without interruption?'. Under 'Distortion' he writes that newspapers, bloggers and apps 'reduced the entire technique to a single instruction: Work for 25 minutes, then take a break', and that 'The iconic 25-minute timer sessions aren't the technique, they're just one expression of this broader mindset'. On goals he writes, 'Even one Pomodoro, or none, is fine. Your goal isn't to complete Pomodoros. Your goal is to become aware of what happens in your mind'. Pomodoro is Italian for tomato.
